newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech PM dispute with c.bank not serious - analysts. [CORRECTED 13:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Czech PM dispute with c.bank not serious - analysts. [CORRECTED 13:20 GMT]

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus's assertion that monetary policy is unduly restrictive does not herald a serious conflict between the central bank and the government, analysts told Reuters on Wednesday.

Speaking to a forum of local business leaders on Tuesday evening, Klaus said that the Czech National Bank (CNB) may have gone too far in its attempts to smother inflation and that the accompanying slowdown in economic growth was too high a price to pay.

"I think that to some extent the development of the conflict is characteristic of many countries - the government is more concerned with growth and the central bank with monetary stability," said Martin Kupka of Patria Finance.
Last summer, the CNB raised the discount rate by one percentage point to 10.5 percent and hiked minimum reserve requirements by 3.5 percentage points to 11.5 percent.
Analysts say this has contributed to a fall in inflation to 7.3 percent year-on-year in February falling compared with an average of 8.8 percent for 1996.

But growth has also fallen steadily, dropping from 4.3 (corrects figure from 4.0) percent in the first quarter of 1996 to 3.6 percent in the third quarter hampering the government in its attempts to balance the state budget. Despite the conflict of priorities, analysts said the central bank's independence would not be compromised.
"Right back in 1991, Vaclav Klaus, then the Finance Minster, strongly supported the idea of an independent central bank," said Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka.
"This is all a quite legitimate discussion as it is between Mr.Tietmeyer and Mr.Waigel," he added, referring to the Bundesbank head and the German Finance Minister respectively.
The Czech prime minister's comments came one day after the CNB said the time was not yet right for a cut in interest rates.
Foreign exchange dealers said the market would attach more weight to the views of the central bank than the prime minister's remarks on Tuesday evening.
"After the speech of (CNB spokesman) Mr. Svehla on Monday many foreign investors bought Czech crowns and the crown appreciated. Right after Klaus, there was no reaction," said Jiri Ubri of ING Bank.

The crown has been steady in quiet trading throughout Wednesday. Just before midday the CNB fixed the Czech currency at 29.116 to the dollar and 17.044 to the mark putting it 2.61 percent above the mid-point of its mark/dollar basket.
